sources.citation: Grambank Consortium. Nyali (nyal1250), coded by Jill Sammet from Harries 1959.https://grambank.clld.org/languages/nyal1250
sources.note: No stress feature; only confirms Harries 1959 as the one usable description.

Alternative names Huku, Linyali, North Nyali, Nyali-Kilo, Nyari; refs Bastin/Coupez/Mann 1999, de Wit 1995, de Wit-Hasselaar 1995 (subclassification only) plus the three descriptive refs in the target record.

sources.citation: Rasmussen, Kent. 2018. A Comparative Tone Analysis of Several Bantu D30 Languages (DR Congo). PhD dissertation, University of Texas at Arlington (Linguistics & TESOL Dissertations 116), 306 pp. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
sources.note: Ch. 5 'Nyali-Kilo [nlj]' (pp. 147-158) describes infinitive-verb tone melodies (Low, High, four depressor-consonant 'Rising' patterns; Table 28 p. 148) from pitch traces, plus D30 consonant/vowel inventories (Tables 3-5). Nothing about word stress in Nyali-Kilo: the full text has 'stress' only at p. 115 ('penultimate word stress', about Ndaka [ndk] 2s-past forms) and in a remark on English orthography. Author states (p. 3) he knows no tone analysis for any Bantu D language except Lika.

tone.says: Ch. 5 groups Nyali-Kilo infinitive verbs into six tone melodies (Table 28, p. 148): Low [333 333 332], High [222 444 444], Low with C1 depressor [444 222 222], High with C1 depressor [222 234 444], Low with C2 depressor [333 333 111], High with C2 depressor [222 444 123]; the four depressor-conditioned melodies are labelled 'Rising'; each class is justified with pitch-trace overlays (Figs. 69-74) and verb lists; 5.6 (pp. 156-157, Table 29) tabulates consonant type ([L/Voice]) against melody: 91…
